done_when: The first close after an upgrade repairs at most the open items and the 20 most recently merged ones, reads no check runs for merged items it repairs, and finishes the repair in minutes on Forge's own repo; later closes do not repeat it; new and existing repos get it on upgrade

known.title: Not done: A retry can repair more than 20 merged items
Not done: Unaffected pull requests consume the merged repair budget
Scale: A fresh checkout still fetches every historical pull request

findings.body:
Gain 3, Work 2, Harm 3
Raise: Test
Case: normal use - an upgrade has an open item and more than 20 merged items needing repair.
The revised test checks the open item's start by decoding the hidden time record and asserting its private event and state fields. It would pass if that record contained the right start while the pull request's visible history still showed the wrong one, and it would fail after a record-format change that preserved the visible behavior. The previously requested check at the user-facing boundary remains missing from this bounded-batch proof.
findings.title: Gate: tests/test_upgrade_start_repair.py::test_1_upgrade_bounds_existing_start_repairs

why: The exact wait-times fix makes the first close after an upgrade repair every past item from the last six weeks: backfill.run rebuilds each pull request whose How it went text says 'nothing running', fetching each old pull request head and its check runs, so on Forge's own repo the first close ran over an hour and spends many GitHub requests
